key_insight: A recurrent ASR system naturally mirrors human auditory cortex organization: different model layers map to distinct cortical regions and together encode a parallel hierarchy of linguistic information from acoustic to phonetic to lexical to semantic levels.
problem_solved: Bridges the gap between computational ASR representations and neural speech processing by identifying how model layers correspond to cortical regions and how linguistic information is organized in the brain.
method: Collect neural responses while humans listen to continuous speech (auditory cortex recordings).
Extract layer-wise activations from a recurrent automatic speech recognition model processing the same stimuli.
Align model and brain representations using representational mapping/encoding analyses to locate which layers correspond to which cortical regions and which linguistic levels they encode.
impact: Provides empirical evidence that brain-inspired, layerwise architectures in ASR reflect human speech processing, guiding interpretable model design and tighter neuro-AI integration for better speech systems and neuroscientific models.
visual_elements: Stacked model-to-brain map: vertical model layers aligned to a lateral brain diagram with colored links showing layer-to-region correspondence.
Parallel pipeline diagram showing progression of information (acoustic → phonetic → lexical → semantic) present in both model and cortex.
Heatmap matrix (model layers × cortical sites) visualizing strength of representational alignment.
Timeline/spectrogram overlay illustrating stimulus, neural responses, and model activations over time.
paper_title: Parallel hierarchical encoding of linguistic representations in the human auditory cortex and recurrent automatic speech recognition systems
paper_authors: Menoua Keshishian, Gavin Mischler, Samuel Thomas, Brian Kingsbury, Stephan Bickel
